titre: Darwin and earthworms: soil plowed before the plow
accroche: In 1842, Darwin spreads chalk over a field. In 1871, it lies 7 inches underground: worms have covered it.
contenu_vulgarise:
On December 20, 1842, Charles Darwin had crushed chalk spread over a field near his house, at Down. It had been pasture for at least thirty years. He wanted to observe, later, how deep the chalk would be buried.

In late November 1871, twenty-nine years later, he had a trench dug across that part of the field. On each side, a line of white nodules appeared 7 inches below the surface, about 18 cm. Fine earth, turf excluded, had therefore accumulated at 0.22 inch per year on average, about 5.6 mm.

## What the worm does

Nobody had turned over this field. Darwin attributes the deposit to an animal we barely look at: the earthworm swallows soil, partly digests it, and ejects it at the surface in small heaps, the castings. Small objects left on the ground end up covered; large stones, Darwin writes, sink slowly by the same process.

He does not stop at one trench. At Stonehenge, beside a fallen stone 17 feet long, he has a hole dug: the layer of humus there measures at least 9.5 inches and the base of the stone lies about 9.5 inches below the level of the neighboring ground. He notes that this stone fell at a remote and unknown time.

To weigh the work, he has the castings collected from a square one yard on a side, on Leith Hill Common, over 367 days. Dried, they weigh 7.453 pounds, which gives, for an acre of the same land, 16.1 (English) tons of dry earth ejected in a year. In the conclusion of his book, he adopts a lower figure: in many parts of England, more than ten tons (10,516 kg) of dry earth pass each year through the bodies of worms, on every acre.

## The shift

The book, *The Formation of Vegetable Mould through the Action of Worms*, appeared on October 10, 1881 from John Murray. Darwin had presented a first paper on the subject to the Geological Society of London on November 1, 1837. His thesis: the entire surface layer of humus passes through the bodies of worms within a few years, and the soil was thus plowed long before humans existed.

For Darwin, topsoil is therefore not an immobile backdrop: its surface layer has passed through the bodies of worms. He pushes the calculation far: ten tons per acre, multiplied by the more than 32 million acres of cultivated land favorable to worms estimated to exist in England and Scotland, then by a million years, gives 320 million million tons of earth. It is an extrapolation, and he himself restricts the ten tons to land that is moist enough, neither too sandy, nor too stony, nor too rocky.

In 1994, Clive Jones, John Lawton, and Moshe Shachak defined ecosystem engineers: organisms that modify, maintain, or create habitats. Darwin mostly measured English fields and reserves his figure for soils where worms live in numbers. What would the same measurement give elsewhere?

repere.texte: A line of chalk spread on December 20, 1842 over a pasture at Down lay, by late November 1871, 7 inches below the surface: fine earth had accumulated above it at 0.22 inch per year on average, in twenty-nine years.
repere.source: Charles Darwin, The Formation of Vegetable Mould through the Action of Worms, with Observations on their Habits, London, John Murray, 1881, chapter III

carte.punch: Darwin spreads chalk in 1842: twenty-nine years later, worms have buried it under 7 inches.
carte.idee: Darwin spreads chalk over a pasture in 1842. Twenty-nine years later, it lies under 7 inches of fine earth ejected by worms. He estimates that, in many parts of England, more than ten tons of earth per acre per year pass through their bodies.

quiz.question: How did the layer of chalk spread in 1842 end up 7 inches below the surface in 1871?
choix: Successive plowings of this field gradually buried it
It sank into the ground by itself, under its own weight
Worms ejected fine earth at the surface, which covered it
quiz.explication: The field had been pasture for at least thirty years, so there was no plow. Darwin reads the line of nodules as a layer covered by the fine earth ejected at the surface by worms, at 0.22 inch per year on average: the chalk did not go down, the earth rose above it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Darwin observe when he has a hole dug beside a fallen stone at Stonehenge?
choix: It is sunk about 9.5 inches below the level of the neighboring ground, covered with humus
The stone rested directly on the chalk of the subsoil, with no layer of earth at all
The ground around the stone had not changed level since its fall
Tree roots had lifted the stone by several inches
quiz_supplementaire.explication: As with the chalk at Down, Darwin reads the partial burial of the stone as the effect of worms: the layer of humus covering it measures at least 9.5 inches, and its base lies at the same depth below the level of the neighboring ground.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Darwin measure the weight of earth that worms eject at the surface, at Leith Hill Common?
choix: He weighs the fine earth removed from a trench dug across an entire acre
He has the castings produced on a square one yard on a side collected over 367 days
He compares the weight of a living worm with that of its castings in one day
He measures the weight loss of a plowed field over ten years
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The castings collected on this square over 367 days weigh, once dry, 7.453 pounds, which gives, scaled to an acre, 16.1 tons of dry earth ejected in a year.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When does Darwin first present his observations on earthworms, before publishing his book in 1881?
choix: In a letter published in Nature in 1859, the year of *On the Origin of Species*
In a lecture at the Royal Society in 1871, the year of the Down trench
In a paper to the Geological Society of London on November 1, 1837
In the preface to the first edition of *On the Origin of Species*
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Darwin had already presented a first paper on the subject in 1837, forty-four years before the full book appeared from John Murray in October 1881.
